title: Iran Declines to Rebuild Nuclear Sites Hit by U.S. Strikes, Says UN Nuclear Chief
body:
Tehran has shown no sign of rebuilding the nuclear installations that were crippled by a series of U.S. and Israeli strikes in 2023 and 2024, the chief of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) told the United Nations Security Council on Tuesday. Rafael Gros, who heads the agency, said satellite imagery, on‑site inspections and intelligence reports all indicate that Iran has not undertaken any repair work at the Natanz enrichment plant, the Fordow underground facility or the Arak heavy‑water reactor complex since the attacks. The absence of reconstruction activity, he added, underscores a “stalemate” in the broader diplomatic impasse over Tehran’s nuclear program.

Gros’s assessment came amid renewed calls from Western powers for Tehran to comply with a series of United Nations resolutions that demand a halt to uranium enrichment and a return to full IAEA safeguards. The United States and Israel have argued that the strikes were necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapons capability, while Tehran maintains that its nuclear activities are peaceful and that the attacks violated international law. By confirming that Iran has not repaired the damaged sites, the IAEA removes one of the key indicators that could have signaled a shift toward a more aggressive nuclear posture.

Analysts note that the lack of repair work may be driven by several pragmatic considerations. First, the technical expertise and specialized components required to restore the sophisticated centrifuge cascades at Natanz and Fordow are not readily available, especially under the weight of sanctions that limit Iran’s access to high‑precision engineering goods. Second, the Iranian leadership may be weighing the political cost of overtly defying the United Nations; any visible reconstruction could be portrayed as a direct provocation, inviting further sanctions or even additional military action. Finally, internal economic pressures—exacerbated by a prolonged downturn in oil revenues—have likely forced Tehran to prioritize domestic needs over costly nuclear infrastructure projects.

The IAEA’s statement also has implications for the diplomatic track that has been pursued behind the scenes. In the months following the 2023 strikes, secret talks in Vienna and Geneva produced a tentative framework for a “comprehensive” deal that would see Iran limit enrichment to 3.67 percent, the level allowed under the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, in exchange for phased sanctions relief. However, the lack of progress on repairs has been cited by Washington and Jerusalem as evidence that Tehran is not fully committed to a return to compliance, complicating the negotiating environment. European diplomats, meanwhile, argue that the very fact Iran has not rebuilt the facilities could be leveraged as a confidence‑building measure, suggesting a window for renewed dialogue.

Regional actors are watching the developments closely. Israel’s defense establishment has warned that any future attempts by Iran to restore its nuclear capabilities will be met with decisive action, while Gulf Cooperation Council states have expressed concern that a revived Iranian program could destabilize the already volatile Middle East. Conversely, Moscow and Beijing have offered diplomatic support to Tehran, framing the strikes as examples of Western aggression and urging a multilateral approach to the nuclear issue. The divergent positions highlight how the nuclear question remains a flashpoint in broader geopolitical rivalries.

Looking ahead, the IAEA’s monitoring will continue to focus on whether Iran initiates any clandestine repair work or shifts its nuclear activities to undisclosed sites. The agency’s next report, due later this year, will be closely scrutinized by the Security Council and could shape the trajectory of future sanctions or diplomatic overtures. If Tehran maintains the status quo, the stalemate may persist, leaving the international community to grapple with a partially crippled but still potentially dangerous nuclear program. Conversely, any move toward reconstruction could reignite a cycle of sanctions, negotiations, and possibly further military confrontations, underscoring the fragile balance that defines the nuclear stalemate in the Middle East.
